what_it_does: AI workloads — things like image recognition, language models, and recommendation systems — require an enormous number of multiply-and-add operations, and running them on traditional electronic chips consumes a lot of power. Photonic computing uses pulses of light instead of electrical signals to perform some of those multiplications, because light can travel through a mesh of optical waveguides (tiny light channels etched into silicon) at very high speed with very little energy. Prior photonic chip proposals focused on the optical math core but left out a realistic design for the supporting memory and data buffering, making them impractical. LightML is claimed to be the first complete system-level design: it pairs the photonic crossbar (a grid where light beams crossing at different angles naturally multiply signals) with a co-designed electronic memory and buffer architecture that keeps the optical core busy more than 80% of the time, delivering 325 tera-operations per second (325 trillion math steps per second) at only 3 watts.
